name: Hiram 'Hy' Tolliver
languages: Spanish (cow-camp Spanish, learned from the vaqueros on the trail: horses, cattle, weather and swearing)
equipment: Leather duster, canvas-lined, with a Company Bar BC brand burned into the collar as a joke by the other hands
Navy revolver (Colt, .36), 6 chambers loaded, his father's
Carbine (Spencer, .56), 7 rounds in the tube, in a saddle scabbard
Horse: Biscuit, a buckskin cow pony, the best cutting horse in the Company's remuda, who belongs to him and not the Company
Lariat (a forty-foot rawhide riata), plus a good Texas saddle, a grass rope, a bridle with a spade bit and a saddle blanket from San Antonio
Leather chaps, spurs with jinglebobs, a slicker and a bedroll
A Company time book showing $40 a month and found, three months unpaid
A hair bridle he is braiding as a present, out of the tail hair of every horse he has broken this spring, which is for Clara Solberg, though nobody knows that
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; half the usual water to avoid thirst one day in three; once per long rest, shrug off a level of exhaustion gained on the trail; rations packed last a day longer)

Saddle-Born (Cowhand: advantage on Riding checks, never disadvantage on ranged attacks from the saddle, mounts and dismounts with 5 ft of movement; his horse Biscuit is part of him: +10 hit points, never spooks under him, comes to his whistle from half a mile and acts on his initiative; proficient with the lariat, and from the saddle he can throw a loop as a bonus action once per turn)
Rawhide (Cowhand: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion, heat and cold; rides 12 hours a day without forced-march saves; spends one extra Hit Die on a short rest)

Cow Sense (Cowhand, 2nd level: advantage on Animal Handling checks with cattle, horses and mules; turns the leaders of a stampede with a single Riding or Animal Handling check as an action, with advantage; a herd he is working never stampedes on a natural 1 or a lightning strike unless someone started it on purpose)

The Trail Outfit (Cattle Drover background: any trail crew, bunkhouse or cow-town saloon takes him in for a night and a short-handed trail boss hires him on sight; he knows the trails, the river crossings and the Association's roundup rules by heart)

personality.traits: I grin at everything and worry at nothing until it is too late. I talk to horses more than people and I think they understand me better. I will ride anything, rope anything and bet on anything, and I am always broke by the second of the month.
personality.ideals: A man's word and a man's horse are the only two things he really owns. The outfit you ride for, you ride for, right or wrong, until it asks you to do something dirty. Then you quit, and you tell them why to their face.
personality.bonds: My uncle Wade, who raised me after my folks died and got me on with the Company. Biscuit. Owen Lasker, who was my friend, whom I taught to throw a loop, and who is dead. And Clara Solberg, whom I am going to marry if her mother and my uncle do not kill us both first.
personality.flaws: I am loyal to the Company because my uncle is, and I have never in my life thought about what the Company is for. I am beginning to, and I do not like it.

appearance: A tall, loose-limbed, sunburned young man of twenty-two with a cowlick of brown hair, a wide easy grin with a chipped front tooth, bowed legs and the long sinewy forearms of a man who has roped a thousand calves. Big hat, jinglebob spurs, a red bandanna, and a buckskin horse that follows him like a dog.
backstory: Hiram Tolliver was born on a ranch on the Llano in Texas in 1864; his father was killed by a horse in 1872 and his mother died of a fever the year after, and his uncle Wade took him on the trail north at ten as a horse wrangler and has never let him out of his sight since. He grew up in the Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company's cow camps, rode his first roundup at fourteen, and is now its best young hand, the one they send for when a horse cannot be broken or a cow cannot be roped. He was friends with Owen Lasker from the day Owen came to the creek in 1883 and asked him, in a terrible Iowa accent, how you throw a loop; they mavericked a few calves together that first year, as every cowboy and homesteader on the range did then, which is now called rustling. Since last autumn he has been meeting Clara Solberg at the Narrows ford on Sunday afternoons. On the night of Sunday 18 April he was at the Forks breaking horses with thirty other riders, and in the morning he heard that Owen was dead with the Association's name on a sign, and the first thing he thought, and is ashamed of thinking, was: did my uncle know? (Suggested employer: the Company, which already pays him. Hooks into the grange: Clara Solberg, Owen's memory, and the fact that he knows the Company did not do it, because he was there.)
